chapter_metadata.description: A structured OSCE abdominal examination guide with image support.

blocks.text: When you begin in an OSCE: RIGHT SIDE OF THE PATIENT

“Hello, I’m a medical student. I’ve been asked to examine your abdomen. This will involve looking, feeling, tapping, and listening to your tummy. It shouldn’t be painful, but let me know if you feel any discomfort.”
Ask about pain → “Do you have any pain?” 👉 If yes → examine painful area LAST

items: 👉 Test: Ask patient to extend arms and dorsiflex wrists

blocks.text: 👉 Warm hands 👉 Kneel or sit at patient level 👉 Watch patient’s face

content_groups.group_title: 👉 This is where many students lose marks — be structured

blocks.text: “On general inspection, the patient appears comfortable at rest with no obvious distress. There are no stigmata of chronic liver disease on the hands, face, or chest.
On abdominal examination, the abdomen is soft and non-distended with no visible scars or masses. There is no tenderness on palpation, and no organomegaly detected.
Percussion reveals normal tympany with no evidence of ascites. Bowel sounds are present and normal.

items: In summary, this is a normal abdominal examination.”

blocks.text: “The abdomen is distended with a full flanks appearance and an everted umbilicus. There are dilated superficial veins visible over the abdominal wall. On palpation, the abdomen is soft and non-tender. Percussion reveals shifting dullness, consistent with free fluid in the abdomen. Bowel sounds are present. These findings are suggestive of ascites, likely secondary to chronic liver disease.”

“On palpation, there is a palpable mass arising from the left costal margin extending towards the right iliac fossa. The mass moves with respiration and has a smooth surface with a palpable notch. I am unable to get above the mass. These findings are consistent with splenomegaly.”

“There is a tender, enlarged liver palpable 3 cm below the right costal margin. The edge is smooth and regular. There is no splenomegaly and no evidence of ascites. These findings suggest hepatomegaly, possibly due to an inflammatory cause such as hepatitis.”

“There are stigmata of chronic liver disease including spider naevi and palmar erythema. The abdomen is distended with evidence of ascites on percussion. The liver edge is not clearly palpable, and there may be splenomegaly. These findings are suggestive of chronic liver disease with portal hypertension.”

“There is localized tenderness in the right iliac fossa with associated guarding. Rebound tenderness is present, and there is maximal tenderness at McBurney’s point. These findings are suggestive of acute appendicitis.”

“There is tenderness in the right upper quadrant with a positive Murphy’s sign. The patient experiences pain and stops inspiration during palpation. These findings are suggestive of acute cholecystitis.”
“There is a central pulsatile abdominal mass located above the umbilicus. The mass is expansile on palpation. These findings are concerning for an abdominal aortic aneurysm.”

“The abdomen is distended with visible peristalsis. On auscultation, there are high-pitched, tinkling bowel sounds. There is generalized tenderness but no peritonism. These findings are suggestive of intestinal obstruction.”
“The abdomen is rigid with generalized tenderness. There is involuntary guarding and rebound tenderness present. Bowel sounds are absent. These findings are consistent with peritonitis.”

“There is a palpable mass in the left lower quadrant measuring approximately 5 cm. It is firm, non-tender, and has limited mobility. The overlying skin appears normal. Further evaluation is required to determine the origin of the mass.”
“There is a mass in the right flank that is ballotable on examination. It is smooth and moves slightly with respiration. These findings are suggestive of a renal mass.”
“There is epigastric tenderness with guarding. There are signs of bruising around the umbilicus (Cullen’s sign). These findings are suggestive of acute pancreatitis, possibly severe.”
“There is a firm, irregular mass palpable in the left iliac fossa. It is non-tender and does not move with respiration. These findings are suggestive of faecal loading.”

“There is a palpable left supraclavicular lymph node. The abdomen shows a possible epigastric mass and features suggestive of ascites. These findings raise suspicion for advanced intra-abdominal malignancy, possibly gastric in origin.”
“There is a swelling in the right inguinal region that becomes more prominent on coughing. It is reducible and has a cough impulse. These findings are consistent with an inguinal hernia.”
Avoid overcommitting: ❌ “This is definitely…” ✅ “Suggestive of / consistent with…”

subsections.subsection_title: Why do you examine the patient from the right side?

blocks.text: It is the standard clinical approach, allowing consistency and easier assessment of organs like the liver, gallbladder, and appendix.

subsections.subsection_title: Why do you ask about pain before examining?

blocks.text: To avoid causing discomfort and to ensure the painful area is examined last, preventing guarding and inaccurate findings.

subsections.subsection_title: Why are your hands warmed before palpation?

blocks.text: Cold hands can cause voluntary guarding, making examination difficult and unreliable.

subsections.subsection_title: What are the causes of abdominal distension?
How do you differentiate ascites from obesity?

blocks.text: Ascites shows shifting dullness and fluid thrill, while obesity does not. The flanks are more full in ascites.
A test for ascites where dullness shifts when the patient changes position, indicating free fluid in the abdomen.

subsections.subsection_title: Why do you auscultate before palpation?

blocks.text: Palpation can alter bowel sounds, so auscultation is done first to assess true bowel activity.
Occur every 5–15 seconds, soft gurgling sounds.

subsections.subsection_title: What do absent bowel sounds suggest?

blocks.text: Paralytic ileus or peritonitis.

subsections.subsection_title: What do hyperactive bowel sounds suggest?

blocks.text: Intestinal obstruction.

subsections.subsection_title: How do you palpate the liver?

blocks.text: Start in the right iliac fossa and move upwards while the patient inspires, feeling for the liver edge.

subsections.subsection_title: What are features of a cirrhotic liver?

blocks.text: Small or enlarged, irregular, nodular, firm, possibly non-tender.

subsections.subsection_title: How do you differentiate liver from spleen enlargement?

items: Spleen: moves diagonally, has a notch, cannot get above it

blocks.text: Pain and arrest of inspiration when palpating the right upper quadrant → suggests acute cholecystitis.
One-third from the ASIS to the umbilicus → site of maximal tenderness in appendicitis.
Pain on release of pressure → indicates peritoneal irritation.
Involuntary contraction of abdominal muscles due to inflammation.

subsections.subsection_title: What is a pulsatile abdominal mass?

blocks.text: Suggestive of an abdominal aortic aneurysm, especially if expansile.
Dilated abdominal veins radiating from the umbilicus due to portal hypertension.

subsections.subsection_title: What are signs of chronic liver disease?

blocks.text: Spider naevi, palmar erythema, ascites, jaundice, gynecomastia, asterixis.

subsections.subsection_title: How do you examine for splenomegaly?

blocks.text: Start in the right iliac fossa and move diagonally towards the left costal margin while patient inspires.
A technique to assess kidneys by trapping them between two hands.
Periumbilical bruising → suggests intra-abdominal bleeding (e.g., pancreatitis).
Flank bruising → retroperitoneal hemorrhage.

subsections.subsection_title: What would you do after completing the abdominal exam?

blocks.text: Examine hernial orifices, perform PR exam if indicated, and check urine.

subsections.subsection_title: How do you examine for ascites clinically?

blocks.text: Shifting dullness and fluid thrill.

subsections.subsection_title: What are the differences between voluntary and involuntary guarding?

items: Voluntary: patient conscious, reduces with relaxation
Involuntary: due to peritonitis, persists despite relaxation

blocks.text: Q: How would you summarize your findings to a consultant?

“This is a patient with abdominal distension, shifting dullness, and stigmata of chronic liver disease, suggestive of ascites likely secondary to liver cirrhosis. I would like to confirm with ultrasound and perform further blood investigations.”
